extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners building or using NLP classifiers to analyze grant peer review reports; funding-agency staff and annotation teams
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and evaluating sentence-level classifiers and an annotation codebook to identify content categories in grant peer review reports (e.g., Track Record, Proposal, Rationale). Includes annotation practice, model fine-tuning, evaluation, and explainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation Criterion (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A top-level dimension grouping review content that evaluates aspects of proposals and applicants (used as categories in the codebook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specific categories such as Track Record; Relevance, Originality, Topicality; Suitability; Feasibility; and Proposal. Table 4 and prevalence statistics show how frequently these appear (e.g. Track Record ~19.6%, Relevance/Originality/Topicality ~17.5%, Suitability ~8.5%, Feasibility ~6.6%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A top-level dimension indicating whether sentences address the proposal, methods, applicant, or applicant quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus categories include Proposal (highest focus ~39.3%), Methods (~16.3%), Applicant (~20.8%) and Applicant: Quantity (~1.1%). Use prevalence measured as number of sentences in category divided by total sentences in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement Type and Reasoning (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dimension capturing the valence of statements (positive/negative), and whether a Rationale is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive sentences outnumber Negative (42.4% vs 17.2% on average). The average review provides a Rationale in 24.4% of sentences classified as positive or negative. Note: Rationale is only considered for Positive or Negative statements in the annotation (see aggregation rule in footnote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Track Record
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that address the applicant's track record, expertise, publications, or research team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: unk, expertise, applicant, dr, publications, experience, track record, field, pi, published, prof, carry, team, 'excellent track record', 'strong track record'. Track Record is the most prevalent Evaluation Criterion (~19.6%). Annotators found this category relatively straightforward (difficulty ~1.75).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance, Originality, Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that comment on the topical fit, novelty, originality, or scientific relevance of the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: originality, original, novel, timely, scientific relevance, topic, relevance, relevant, innovative, highly relevant, novelty, potential, interesting. Prevalence ~17.5%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that evaluate whether chosen methods or approaches are suitable to answer research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: methods, suitability, proposed methods, methodology, methods proposed, well suited, suited, method, answering, chosen methods, adequate, feasible, sample size, approach. Prevalence ~8.5%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that assess whether the project milestones, timeline, workload, budget, personnel and resources make the project achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms: feasible, feasibility, milestones, timeline, workload, project, budget, personnel, planned duration, schedule, achievable, reasonable, time, realistic, available resources. Prevalence ~6.6% and this category was among the harder-to-classify (class imbalance impacted accuracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad category covering sentences that address the proposed project, research plan, aims, or overall application content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: project, proposal, originality, topic, topicality, scientific relevance, timely, ambitious, overall, aims, research plan. Proposal is the single most prevalent Focus (~39.3%). The category is broad and produced lower inter-coder agreement and classification difficulty due to overlap with Methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that specifically discuss methodological approaches, experiments, models, data, sampling, measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: methods, method, use, using, methodology, approach, experiments, model, samples, sample size, data, sampling, measurements. Methods prevalence ~16.3%. Annotators sometimes found distinguishing Methods vs Proposal difficult in some fields (social sciences/humanities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that address the applicant in general (team, institutions, collaborators, expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: unk, team, prof, track record, field, carry, expert, applicants, professor, university, collaborators, publications, research. Prevalence ~20.8%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that make quantitative assessments about applicants (publication counts, h-index, citations, bibliometrics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: published, h-index, publications, papers, citations, google scholar, scopus. This category is rare (~1.1% prevalence). The paper notes that quantitative bibliometric assessments were uncommon and referenced DORA as context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive (statement type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that express praise, endorsement, or positive evaluation of aspects of the proposal or applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: expertise, excellent, strong, timely, outstanding. Positive sentences average ~42.4% of sentences. ~67% of positive/negative statements included a Rationale in the annotated subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative (statement type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that express criticism, concerns, weaknesses, or negative evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: lack, unclear, weakness, limited, concern, missing, vague, lacking. Negative sentences average ~17.2% of sentences and show skewed distribution across reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification or reasoning offered for a positive or negative statement (i.e., explanation supporting praise or criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale was annotated only for sentences that were Positive or Negative. The survey found Rationale the most challenging category to annotate (difficulty ~7.25) and it had the lowest F1 scores. In aggregation: if a sentence is not classified as Positive or Negative, its Rationale prediction is disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that offer suggestions, recommendations, or advice for improving the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive terms include: helpful, better, suggest, recommend, strengthened, useful, consider, strengthen, clearer, encourage, might, stronger. Suggestions are infrequent in grant peer review reports (~4.1% prevalence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of Category (measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: How common a category is within a review: measured as number of sentences classified as the category divided by total number of sentences in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can exceed 100% across all categories because sentences may be multi-labeled. Used to compare annotated sample proportions to full-corpus predictions (reported correspondence r = 0.99). Prevalence correlates with classifier F1 for some approaches but not for the binary classifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro F1 Score (performance metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Macro-averaged F1 score across classes used to evaluate classifier accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in cross-validation and ablation studies. The paper reports relationships between Macro F1 and category prevalence, and shows binary classifiers' F1 was relatively independent of prevalence. Figures show macro F1 per classifier and category; use Pearson correlations to assess relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived difficulty of annotating category
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators rated ease/difficulty on a scale from 1 (very straightforward) to 10 (very challenging); average difficulty scores used to interpret classifier performance and annotation challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average difficulty across categories was 3.73, median 3.50. Track Record scored ~1.75 (easy), Rationale ~7.25 (challenging). Categories easier for annotators generally had higher F1 scores (r = -0.73 between perceived difficulty and F1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-coder agreement and training-data composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of majority voting versus unanimous agreement when constructing training labels, and the effect of restricting to full-agreement sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifiers trained only on unanimous (full-agreement) sentences performed slightly better for categories with lower intercoder agreement (e.g., Proposal, Positive) but worse for categories like Applicant: Quantity and Feasibility. Overall, restricting training to full-agreement sentences did not significantly improve overall performance; majority-vote with more data was advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: sentence-level
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic unit for annotation and classification is the individual sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence-level analysis was effective overall. A test adding surrounding sentences (Rationale and Context) did not improve classification accuracy for Rationale (F1 0.71 for both), and in cross-validation the model trained on only the target sentence tended to outperform the context-inclusive model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-set size and ablation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How model performance depends on the amount of annotated training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ablation study fine-tuned SPECTER2 with increments of 500 sentences up to 2,500. For balanced/moderately imbalanced categories, small annotated samples already yielded high accuracy and additional data gave marginal gains. For highly imbalanced categories (e.g., Feasibility, Suggestion), additional training data substantially improved performance until around ~2,000 annotated sentences, after which gains were minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of classification approach (binary vs multi-label vs multi-task)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting modelling strategy affects performance and relationship to prevalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary classifiers outperformed multi-label and multi-task methods in this study. Binary classifier performance was unrelated to category prevalence or label imbalance (supporting choosing the binary classifier). Researchers should compare modelling approaches rather than over-optimizing model choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability via keyness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Using keyness (chi-squared) analysis on predicted positives vs negatives to identify terms predictive of each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper applied keyness analysis to 1,612,405 sentences to surface the most predictive terms/expressions for each category (Table 4 lists top 25). This provides face validity and insight into what the classifier uses to predict categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LLM few-shot annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating labeled data via few-shot prompting to augment training data or classifying directly with LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tested Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct with tailored prompts and example positive/negative sentences. LLMs performed poorly, especially on imbalanced categories, and lagged behind fine-tuned transformer models. Recommendation: do not include LLM-generated labels or use LLMs directly for classification without validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator selection and instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing and instructing annotators for manual labeling using the codebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators in this study were academics familiar with peer review though not domain experts. Instructed non-expert annotators often adhere closely to the codebook and can perform comparably to experts (Snow et al., 2008). Working in a team and refining the codebook is critical to handle jargon, implicit meanings, and vague texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability / trustworthiness and deployment safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements and cautions before deploying automated classification of peer review reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select classifiers based on quantitative metrics (accuracy thresholds) and qualitative assessments (systematic deviations from human annotations). Classifiers should not be used for automatic classification of grant peer review reports without human oversight; evaluate classification accuracy critically before deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to funder guidelines and avoidance of bibliometric emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative norm/guideline that peer review reports should align with the funder's objectives and avoid undue emphasis on bibliometric indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper notes SNSF Project Funding is project-centered and that quantitative bibliometric assessments (publication counts, h-index, citation counts) were uncommon, consistent with DORA commitments. Analyses of review content should consider alignment with funder requirements and research-assessment policies.
